text: assertEqual works when a function returns a deterministic value. A quantum circuit's measurement outcome is a random sample from a distribution — testing it requires a different vocabulary entirely, and conflating the two is the single most common quantum-testing mistake.

This lesson covers the two genuinely different categories of quantum test, why 'the test passed once' and 'the test is correct' are not the same claim for a probabilistic system, what a flaky statistical test actually means and how to fix it, and how the rest of this chapter builds: construction tests, statistical tests, debugging, then a hands-on lab.

Every test you write against quantum code falls into one of two categories. Construction tests are deterministic checks of the circuit before it's run — gate count, qubit count, which parameters are bound where. These use ordinary exact-equality assertions, because circuit construction is deterministic code, no different from testing a function that builds a list. Statistical tests check measurement outcomes after running some number of shots, and they can never use exact equality, because the outcome is a random sample.

It's tempting to think quantum code needs every test to be statistical. That's wrong. Testing that an oracle produces a circuit with exactly three qubits and the right pattern of X gates marking a specific bitstring is a construction test — nothing here is probabilistic. The oracle either has the right gates on the right qubits or it doesn't, and this test should pass or fail identically on every single run.

A statistical test that passed on one run tells you less than a construction test that passed once. Construction tests are deterministic — if they pass, they'll pass identically on every future run against unchanged code. A statistical test's single pass is itself a sample: correct code can occasionally produce a false negative by design, and subtly broken code can occasionally produce a false positive. That's why statistical tests need a stated confidence level — an explicit acknowledgment that the test itself has a known, calculated error rate.

If a statistical test fails intermittently on unchanged code, the instinct to just re-run it is exactly backwards. Intermittent failure on correct code means your tolerance is too tight for your shot count — a test design bug, not a fluke to ignore. The fix is either loosen the confidence threshold to match the stakes, or increase the shot count so sampling noise shrinks, both concrete, calculable choices rather than crossing your fingers.

Lesson 6 goes deep on construction tests. Lesson 7 builds the statistical-testing toolkit with a worked, verified numeric example. Lesson 8 covers debugging when results are wrong. And lesson 9 is a hands-on lab combining all three into a real test suite.
